cards.title: Back-in-stock scarcity ads and comment mining
cards.summary: Use sold-out/restock messaging and customer comment sections to build authentic scarcity creative for ecommerce brands.
cards.use_when: Planning acquisition creative for a product that has sold out or restocked, or when you need low-cost ad concepts that signal real demand.
steps: Build a restock ad by leading with the fact that the product sold out (source example: 'This anti-aging serum sold out three times this year, and here's why people are raving about it').
Mine your own product comments and DMs for organic demand signals, e.g. customers commenting 'when is the restock, please' — screenshot or film these and use them directly in the ad.
Show the comment thread on screen as the hook so the scarcity proof is visible, not just claimed.
Pair the restock message with the reason people wanted it back (a specific benefit or review), so the ad is not only scarcity.
If the product is genuinely out of stock, run waitlist or back-in-stock notification creative to capture demand instead of pausing spend entirely.
caveats: Only use restock/sold-out claims you can substantiate; the source presents these as common patterns, not as verified performance guarantees.
Scarcity wears out — rotate restock angles so the claim stays credible.

cards.title: Stack social proof in the first seconds of ad creative
cards.summary: Layer reviews, real-customer footage and follower counts into ads to lift credibility and performance.
cards.use_when: Producing ad creative for a PDP-driven campaign where you need higher trust and click-through on cold audiences.
steps: Add on-screen review cards (star ratings, quotes, before/after photos) over the product footage rather than relying on spoken claims alone.
Film or source real customer conversations — interview an actual buyer about the product and use their words as the ad script.
Include measurable authority signals where true, e.g. on-screen mention of follower counts like 90K Instagram followers, or the number of customers served.
Use founder/customer pregnancy, skin, fitness or lifestyle stories as testimonial narrative arcs, since the source shows these being used as identifiable real-person formats.
Match the social-proof format to the placement: short review overlays for cold traffic, long testimonial narrative for retargeting.
caveats: The source states more social proof tends to perform better but gives no benchmark; treat as a directional principle.
Never fabricate review counts or before/after results — social proof that can't be verified exposes the store to ad rejection and refunds.

cards.title: Specificity principle for claim writing
cards.summary: Replace vague benefit claims with precise numbers, timeframes and percentages to make ad copy and PDP claims believable.
cards.use_when: Writing ad hooks, PDP headlines, bullets or email subject lines where claims currently sound generic and are being ignored.
steps: Audit each claim for specificity: vague claims get ignored; specific claims get believed (source rule).
Convert rounded/vague numbers into exact ones — source examples: 'lose weight fast' becomes 'lose 11 lb in 23 days'; 'boost your income' becomes 'made $4,387 in 12 days'.

For ecommerce, apply the same to product claims: '98% natural' instead of '100% natural' reads as more believable (source example), and day-by-day results ('watch how this changed my skin in 2 weeks') beat a single generic after shot.
Use numbered day or result progressions in creative (day 0 through day 20) to show the timeline behind the claim.
For stats-based hooks, use specific failure or success rates to create curiosity, e.g. the source's example referencing a percentage of coconut oil products failing.
Apply the same rewriting pass to PDP bullets and bundle descriptions so ad and landing page claims stay consistent.
caveats: Specific claims still need to be truthful and substantiated; the source is describing persuasive framing, not permission to invent numbers.
Odd, precise numbers feel more credible than round ones, but don't fabricate precision you can't back up.

cards.title: Using TikTok Creative Center top ads for swipe files
cards.summary: Search and filter TikTok's free ads library to collect hook and format inspiration, while accounting for opt-in limitations.
cards.use_when: Sourcing ad inspiration or competitor research before shooting a new batch of TikTok creatives for your product category.
steps: Go to TikTok Creative Center and open the Ads Inspiration / Top Ads dashboard; verify the current navigation since TikTok's interface changes.
Filter minimally: the source recommends just country plus niche/industry, because each additional filter (including objective) narrows the pool of visible ads.
Set the date range to the last 180 days to maximize the number of ads returned.
Leave ad format open unless you specifically need one format; then sort by likes (e.g. top 1–20%) to surface the strongest performers.
Open the analytics panel on any ad to see likes, CTR, budget tier and the landing page URL — the landing page is useful for copying page structure, not just the creative.
Save ads into named collections inside Creative Center so swipe files stay organized by product or angle.
Use the keyword search for a specific term (e.g. 'protein'), but expect buggy or thin results for very niche keywords.
caveats: Ads only appear if the advertiser opted in; many large-spend brands deliberately opt out, so this library is not comprehensive.
High likes does not equal high purchase conversion — treat it as format/hook inspiration, not proof of sales performance.

cards.title: TikTok One top ads insight for category creative angles
cards.summary: Use TikTok One's creative library and top-ads insight panel to extract category-level selling points and audience angles.
cards.use_when: Deciding which creative angles and selling points to test for a category (e.g. beauty, personal care) on TikTok Shop.
steps: Access TikTok One via the prompt inside Creative Center or via ad account > Tools > Creative Inspiration; use Explore Mode for the full library view.
Open Top Ads Insight and filter by category, region and a 30-day window.
Set the sort to top video views to see which creative approaches dominate that niche.

Use the breakdown table that lists target audience, physical product, applicable scenarios and specific selling points with example ads, and turn each selling point into a testable hook for your own product.
Cross-reference these angles with your own reviews and comments to pick which ones fit your product truthfully.
Re-check the tool periodically: the source notes some views (e.g. the creative-approach panel) were behaving unreliably at recording time.
caveats: The source found the overlap with Creative Center data high and some panels buggy or in rollout; verify what's currently functional before relying on it.
Selling-point examples are category-level inspiration, not validated results for your product.

cards.title: Organized ad swipe files with a paid ad-spy tool
cards.summary: Build boards of competitor and category ads with a paid library that captures opted-out ads and offers strong search.
cards.use_when: Running frequent creative testing and needing a persistent, searchable swipe file across TikTok and other platforms, including competitor accounts.
steps: Choose the tool if you are producing ads regularly (the source calls it not worth it for one-off advertisers) and set up boards by angle, competitor or campaign, e.g. separate boards for each psychological principle, seasonal events like Black Friday, and each client.
Use filters to narrow by platform, format (video vs image) and niche, then apply to build a filtered feed of relevant ads.
Search by product keyword; the source reports noticeably better results than the free TikTok keyword search.
Spy on a specific brand to see all ads they are currently running across platforms, then save individual ads into the relevant board.
Review boards before each new creative sprint to pick angles and formats you haven't tested yet.
caveats: Paid tool; the source's preference is personal and based on frequent ad production, not a universal recommendation.
Tool names, pricing and interfaces change — verify current plans and features before subscribing.

cards.title: TikTok Shop product research with Kalodata
cards.summary: Use TikTok Shop sales data to find and validate products before committing to ad spend.
cards.use_when: Selecting which product to launch or source for a TikTok Shop store, before building creative or landing pages.
steps: Open the shop tab and filter/sort by items sold to see which brands and products are currently moving volume on TikTok Shop.
Inspect a specific seller to see recent unit sales — the source's example brand sold 384+ items in 30 days (treat as a point-in-time example, not a benchmark).
Shortlist products whose category and price point match your fulfillment and margin constraints.
Take the shortlisted brand into an ad-spy tool to see which ads are driving their sales, so you know the creative format before you commit.
Free plan limits searches per day (source example: 10 searches/day), so plan which products and categories to look up before starting.
caveats: The source finds this more useful for product selection than for ongoing ad inspiration, and doesn't pay for it personally — it's presented as an alternative, not a required tool.
Past 30-day sales don't guarantee future demand; watch for saturated categories before launching.

cards.title: Three ad production options: DIY, UGC creators, AI
cards.summary: Compare the cost, speed, scalability and conversion trade-offs of in-house, creator and AI-produced TikTok ads.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to resource a new batch of TikTok ad creative when you have limited budget and time.
steps: Option 1 — DIY: cheapest and lets you make real-time edits based on in-account data and swap hooks fast; cons are effort (scripting, filming, editing) and scalability depends on your editing skill. Source recommends CapCut for this path.

Option 2 — hire UGC creators: source says typically best converting because UGC creators convert well, and it is highly scalable; cons are cost. Source recommends marketplaces like Viral Ecom Ads or Fiverr.

Option 3 — AI: fastest and very scalable with a small learning curve; traditionally framed as lowest converting, though the source claims newer AI tools are now among the better converters. Source recommends Creatify and Arc Ads.
Run a small test batch per method and compare against the same product and offer before reallocating budget.
Match method to testing stage: DIY/AI for rapid hook iteration, creators for proven angles you want to scale.
caveats: Conversion ranking (UGC > AI) is the source's stated industry assumption with the caveat that AI is closing the gap; not a universal benchmark.
Cost examples for creator packages vary by vendor — confirm current pricing and deliverables.

cards.title: Script and shoot a problem-solution ad yourself
cards.summary: Write a UGC-style script and film it in segments on a phone for fast, low-cost ad testing.
cards.use_when: Producing first-party ad creative for a product demo when budget doesn't allow creators.
steps: Follow the eight-step formula from the source's earlier module: hook, problem, failed solution (optional), intro, product, features, benefits, demo, desired result.

Generate or write a script around a specific problem and solution — e.g. provide a prompt like 'Create a UGC-style script for [product] that focuses on the problem-solution. One problem with other [category] is [X]. This one is not.' and let Claude or ChatGPT produce hook, problem, product intro, demo, payoff and CTA sections with visual suggestions.
Film each segment separately on a vertical phone: record the hook, pause, then record problem, then product intro, feature/benefit, and call to action as distinct clips.
Change angle or background roughly every 3 seconds so something new is on screen through the ad (source's stated pacing preference).
Optional hardware: a tripod if you don't want to hold the phone; nothing more is strictly needed.
caveats: The output is a raw demo, not a polished commercial — the source presents it as a realistic starting point.
Hook pacing rules are stated heuristically, not derived from tested platform data.

cards.title: CapCut assembly workflow for TikTok ads
cards.summary: Cut dead space, enhance audio, add text, sound effects, music and captions to assemble a vertical ad in CapCut.
cards.use_when: Editing a filmed or AI-generated ad for TikTok to meet platform pacing and accessibility norms.
steps: Import all clips in intended order, then zoom out on the timeline so you can see audio waveforms and dead space between takes.
Cut dead space at the start and between clips so the video begins directly on speech; the source notes TikTok videos shouldn't have leading silence.

Highlight a clip and use CapCut's enhanced-audio options (noise reduction, voice enhance, loudness normalize) — source says these are paid features — to smooth audio peaks and echo from phone recording.
Add a hook text overlay at the start ('Tired of chalky protein?') so viewers scrolling muted understand the video; keep the text up only for the hook segment rather than the whole ad.
Drop a sound effect (e.g. camera click) and a visual sticker (circle/arrow) exactly at the moment a key claim is spoken, so the claim is highlighted visually and audibly.
Add background music from the commercial-use filter only, then lower its volume so it sits just barely behind the voice.
Generate captions, review for false filler-word removals, adjust position so captions don't cover product details, and pick a caption template for readability.
caveats: Some features (audio enhancement, caption generation) require the paid plan — the source notes roughly $20/month; verify current pricing.
Filtering music to commercial sounds is essential for ads; unfiltered music risks copyright issues when the video runs as an ad.
Auto-caption filler detection is imperfect — the source shows 'like' being flagged when it wasn't filler.

cards.title: Add B-roll to hold attention in short-form ads
cards.summary: Overlay supporting footage on top of talking-head segments to keep viewers watching and illustrate claims.
cards.use_when: Editing a talking-head ad that risks losing viewers during explanation or demo segments.
steps: Place B-roll on the timeline above the main video track so it overlays rather than replaces the speaker (placing it below will take over that segment).
Scale the B-roll clip to fill the frame, and align its timing with the spoken line it illustrates — e.g. footage of someone eating chalk over the line about chalky protein.
Mute the B-roll clip's own audio completely via its audio tab, otherwise it fights the voice track.
Check that captions sit above the B-roll layer so text stays visible; adjust caption placement if the overlay covers them.
Add B-roll at multiple points — the source recommends more rather than fewer cuts to maintain attention.
caveats: The source's 'more B-roll keeps attention' guidance is presented as experience, not a tested threshold.
Track ordering in CapCut controls visibility; verify layer order before exporting.

cards.title: Hiring UGC creators through marketplaces
cards.summary: Brief and buy creator ad packages that test multiple hooks, using marketplaces with transparent pricing.
cards.use_when: Scaling creative volume after an angle works, or when you don't want to appear on camera yourself.
steps: Use a marketplace like Viral Ecom Ads for quick turnaround, or Fiverr where you can screen individual creators and see pricing up front.

Start with a small multi-hook package rather than a large one — the source recommends beginning with the three-pack (bundle of hook variations) before committing more, e.g. three-pack pricing cited around $180 versus five-pack around $300.

For Fiverr, read each gig's package terms carefully: the source's example creator offered one video with no copyright usage for $50, scaling to around $100 for copyright-provided or premium tiers — confirm usage rights before purchase, especially for paid ad rights.
Decide the level of direction: supply an exact script, or let the creator use their own judgment for a more native feel.
Expect to ship the product to the creator and allow back-and-forth on creative direction before delivery.
Organize delivered videos by hook and angle in your swipe file so you can test them systematically.
caveats: Pricing figures are the source's point-in-time examples and vary by creator and package.
Usage rights and whitelisting permissions differ per gig — verify what you're licensed to run as a paid ad.

cards.title: Generate AI talking-actor ads with emotion tagging
cards.summary: Create AI spokesperson videos in Arc Ads with script, actor selection, emotion prompts and model choice.
cards.use_when: Producing a high volume of talking-head ad variants fast, when real creators are too slow or expensive.
steps: Create a project inside a named folder organized by video type so outputs stay sortable.
Choose the AI actor option in the project interface; this format suits a script-only talking head where the actor isn't holding or using the product.
Paste your script, then select an actor by filtering all/favorites/my actors and gender, age or background scene.
Select multiple actors at once if you want the same script generated with several faces for A/B testing. The source says you can add three actors and each will generate the script.
Add emotions automatically and review them — the tool detects lines as excited, mischievous, satisfied, etc., which the source says makes delivery less robotic; you can edit individual lines.
Pick the model (source compares Arc Ads 1.0 vs Omni Human 1.5) and whether to use standard text-to-speech or speech-to-speech if you want your own recorded inflection.
Generate and expect roughly 1 credit per video; generation typically takes a few minutes in the source's demo.
caveats: The source warns some features produce sub-par results and can waste credits — test a single video before batch generating.
Model and interface options change; verify current model names and credit costs before spending.
AI talking heads are not shown holding the product in this format — use the product-showcase preset for that.

cards.title: AI fashion try-on ads from product photos
cards.summary: Generate realistic model try-on videos from a clothing product image using Arc Ads presets.
cards.use_when: Selling apparel and needing model footage in many styles or scenes without booking shoots.
steps: Open the project's 'see more' menu and choose presets, then select the fashion try-on preset.
Pick a scene preset (e.g. the closet setup the source demonstrates) and click remix to load it.
Upload your own product image of the garment.
Choose the aspect ratio — 9:16 for vertical TikTok output; leave it vertical for ads.
Generate the video and review; the source notes the output looked ultra-realistic with the actor wearing the uploaded product.
Export the try-on clip and combine it with other assets, e.g. a separate talking-actor clip, to build a fuller ad in your editor.
caveats: Each generation consumes credits; the source recommends testing outputs before batch runs.
Output quality depends on the product image you upload; the source's other preset (product showcase) requires clean white-background images.

cards.title: AI product-showcase ads with actor holding your SKU
cards.summary: Generate AI actor videos holding or using a physical product from a clean product image plus a written direction.
cards.use_when: Advertising a physical product that isn't apparel and you need demonstration footage without a shoot.
steps: Open 'see more' > presets and choose the product showcase preset rather than fashion try-on.
Select the scene preset closest to your desired setting (e.g. a bedroom) and click remix; note you will get a different actor than the preset shows.
Upload your product photo — the source stresses it should be on a white background with no people in the image for best results.
Set the aspect ratio to 9:16 for vertical ad placements.
Write a description of the action you want: the source's example tells the model to sit as shown while holding the charger and talk about how great it is for charging her phone and other devices.
Generate the video (the source notes roughly one credit and a few minutes waiting) and review whether the actor appears to hold/use the product convincingly.
Export and edit together with talking-head or B-roll clips for a complete ad.
caveats: The resulting actor won't match the preset actor shown in the library.
The source says generation typically takes around two to five minutes, so batch planning matters when testing many angles.
Image cleanliness strongly affects output — crowded or people-containing product photos are explicitly discouraged.
